newsitem.title: USA: Mark may gain from German Court EMU opt-out rule.
newsitem.headline: Mark may gain from German Court EMU opt-out rule.

text.p: The mark may get a boost from a 1993 German Constitutional Court ruling that gives Germany an opt-out of the European Monetary Union (EMU) if the Maastricht criteria are diluted, U.S. analysts said.
"They (the Germans) could clearly get out of the EMU. The ruling gives them a way out," said David De Rosa, managing partner at Quadrangle Investments, a hedge fund.
De Rosa was referring to an October 1993 ruling by the Constitutional Court, Germany's highest court, that gave the nation the right to withdraw from the EMU at any time.

In an answer to a challenge that the Maastricht Treaty threatened Germany's sovereignty, the Constitutional Court ruled in 1993 that Germany "is not subordinating itself to an unclear, automatic and uncontrollable mechanism leading to currency union."

De Rosa said sentiment in the market is that there is "sympathy being shared between the Constitutional Court and the Bundesbank for a tough stand on the EMU, in particular a strict upholding of the stability pact."
"The real choker is that the court made clear the European members cannot dilute the criteria," De Rosa added.

The 1993 Constitutional Court ruling said that -- if the Maastricht criteria were relaxed -- Germany's participation in the single European currency would require new approval by the German parliament. The euro is scheduled for January 1, 1999.

"If the institutions of the European Community interpret or implement in any other way, then their action would not be in conformity with the law of ratification in Germany and thus not legally binding within the German member state," the Court ruling said.
Private forecasts indicate Germany and France are unlikely to meet the Maastricht debt criteria by 1999.

Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the "1993 ruling has paved the way for further challenges," adding that he expected fresh constitutional challenges to Germany's participation in the euro.

"The D-mark stability is enshrined in the German Constitution. Some people may argue the Maastricht Treaty, as it is unfolding, is challenging the D-mark strength and therefore that the Treaty should be overruled on constitutional ground," Chandler said.
But Chandler said the Constitutional Court is unlikely to seek the final say on the issue.
"There is a difference of opinion between the Bundesbank and the government," said Chandler, who predicted the disagreement will probably be resolved later this week.
Chandler said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell was predicting the euro will start on time -- but be weakened.
Senior analyst Kevin Harris at MCM CurrencyWatch said some former Bundesbank members spoke about again challenging the Maastricht Treaty in the Constitutional Court.
"They have threatened to challenge the Treaty for some time. Now that Germany will be less than pristine for entry in the euro, the threat is more relevant," Harris added.

Harris said prospects of a delay in the euro timetable "is a plus for the mark on the short term," though he expected the mark to weaken mainly versus the dollar as it becomes clear the euro would start on time but in a watered-down form.

"By the time all of this would happen, one year from now, Germany may be back raising interest rates again. It's difficult to predict the strength of the D-mark then," added Harris, who expected interest rate differentials to play a greater role in the foreign exchange picture once the outlook for the euro is more certain.
